body: At five in the morning, in the shared kitchen of a hostel for agricultural workers, a man of about thirty is waiting for a kettle and for a minibus, in that order. He has eleven minutes. He props his phone against the sugar tin and goes looking for something to have on while he eats, and what he finds is worship in English, which he follows about half of, and worship in Hindi, which is near enough to be maddening — the shape of it is right and the words belong to somebody else. He plays the Hindi one. He turns it down when the others come in. On the bus he does not think about it again.

Nothing went wrong there. A man wanted God addressed in the language he thinks in before his day started, and what he got was close. Close is a real thing and it is worth having, and it is not the thing.

There are 29 languages on this band besides English, carried by 40 stations. That is a real number and it is also a small one, set against roughly seven thousand living languages and the several hundred with more than a million speakers apiece.

The word missing is doing more work here than absent would, and it is worth taking literally. Absent is a description of a shelf. Missing is a description of somebody who is expected and has not arrived, and that is the accurate word for this, because a language is not a market segment and it is not a checkbox on a plan. It is the only set of sounds in which a particular grandmother has ever thought anything through. She can be reached in her second language the way you can be reached through a wall — she will get the sense of it, and she will not be sung to. What is missing from this dial is not coverage. It is her.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, of which 46 are on air today. The international frequencies sit together in their own stretch of the band, and every one of them is hosted in its language rather than translated into it afterwards.

So the list of what is not here is published beside the list of what is, which is not the usual arrangement and is not a comfortable one. There is nothing yet in Urdu, in Farsi, in Burmese, in Hausa, in Igbo, in Malay, in Nepali, in Somali, in Pashto, in Tamil, in Khmer or in Zulu, and that is not the list, it is the beginning of one. A gap nobody names is a gap nobody fills. Naming it is the cheapest part of filling it, and it is the part almost nobody does.

Almost every organisation doing this work publishes the opposite document. You are shown the countries reached, the languages added this year, the map with the pins in it, and never the map with the holes in it, because the second map is a confession and the first is a poster. Nobody is lying. It is what happens when an institution has to be encouraging in order to be funded, and the cost is that the people who could actually help — the ones who speak the missing language and have wondered for years why nobody asked them — never find out they were needed.

The band is arranged so that a language arrives as a whole address rather than as a feature. It is given a frequency of its own in the international stretch, a host who speaks it, and, in time, its own prayer frequency alongside the music. That is a far heavier commitment than adding a filter to a catalogue, and it is deliberately heavier, because a number that has been given to a language cannot quietly be taken back when the enthusiasm passes.
None of which is an argument against translation. It is an argument about what translation can and cannot carry.

Be fair to it first. Translated hymns have carried the gospel across more borders than any other method, and a subtitle at the bottom of a screen has done more good in twenty years than most of us will manage in a lifetime. But a song is not a container that words are poured into. The metre belongs to the language. So does the rhyme, and so does the particular way grief sounds when it is sung by people who have grieved in that tongue for four hundred years. Run a chorus through a translator and the meaning survives while the fit is destroyed, and everyone singing it can hear that it was made somewhere else and posted to them.
A translated song is a report of worship. It is not worship happening.

In a church hall on a Sunday, after everybody else has gone through for tea, a woman of sixty is still sitting in the third row with her coat on, and her daughter is beside her going back through the sermon in Somali, a sentence at a time, from memory. They have done this for years. The daughter gets a phrase wrong and they both laugh at it, and she tries again. Then she stops, because she has come to a word she has only ever had in English, and she does not know what her mother would call it, and her mother does not know either, because nobody has ever sung it to her. They sit with that for a moment. Then they go through for tea.
That is the gap, and it is not a scheduling problem. A word never sung in a language is a word that language has not been handed, and goodwill in another tongue does not put it there.

Which is why some of these will stay on the list a long time, and it would be dishonest to imply otherwise. Money does not solve a language with little written worship tradition to draw on. Such a language needs people inside it who know it well enough to say whether what comes out of the other end is actually right, and those people are not commissioned, they are found. Some of the names above will still be here in five years. That is the plain truth of it, written down on purpose.

But a published list is a different object from a private intention. An intention costs nobody anything; it can be revised quietly in a meeting and no one outside the room is any the wiser. A list on a public page can be pointed at. It can be shortened, and it can be checked. It is the difference between hoping a language is coming and seeing, this afternoon, whether it has. Being held to something is not a burden here. It is the only mechanism that has ever reliably got anything finished.

So the measure of whether this band is working is not how many frequencies are lit. Frequencies are easy to add and easier to announce. The measure is whether the list of what is missing is shorter than last year, and whether the languages coming off it are the difficult ones rather than the convenient ones. Every name on that list is somebody expected who has not arrived.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial and it helps to know they are there. Most of the band is music — worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there is the international stretch, where each language has its own frequency and its own host, and where the stations are not versions of an English one with the vocals swapped. Turning through that stretch is the quickest way to hear what this article has been arguing.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 334.40 — Asia Inspire, the Mandarin flagship, house-church-friendly worship and teaching for the mainland, Taiwan, Hong Kong and the diaspora. Put it on even though you almost certainly do not speak a word of it, because that is exactly the point of listening to it. What you are hearing is what a filled gap sounds like from the outside: a room of people being sung to in the language they think in, with nobody translating and nobody apologising for it. Then think of a language that is not on this dial at all, and imagine that frequency silent. That silence is the whole subject of this article.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have, which matters a great deal for most of the languages still to come. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation with a task attached, which is unusual for an article of this kind. Put HM 334.40 on this afternoon and listen to a language you do not have. Then, if the tongue of your mother or your neighbour or the man waiting for the minibus is not on this dial, say so out loud, to somebody who can do something about it. Every frequency on this band began as a name that somebody bothered to speak. A gap nobody names is a gap nobody fills, and the naming is the part you can do today.
